title: Replicated log with Raft (simplified): terms, commit index, re-election, election restriction
description: Three Raft nodes on a deterministic simulated network elect a leader, replicate and commit a log, survive a leader crash — then a stale follower wins an election and erases committed entries until you add the election restriction.
outcome: You can explain and trace Raft's election, replication and commit rules, spot a lost committed entry with a safety checker, and implement the up-to-date vote check from the Raft paper.
environment: Python 3.12 (validated on 3.12.15, Linux), stdlib only, no installs beyond lesson 1; macOS (Apple silicon) and Windows 11: same commands (env-var syntax differs, see steps). Optional: Maelstrom 0.2.4 (JDK 11+) for the Raft chapter (manual).
overview: A majority-replicated log stays correct through crashes only if a voter refuses candidates with older logs; without that one check, a node that missed committed writes can become leader and overwrite them.
prerequisites: Lesson 6 (Lamport clocks: terms are a logical clock)

glossary.meaning: Raft's logical clock: each election starts a new, higher term; at most one leader per term.
Highest log index known to be stored on a majority (from the leader's current term); safe to apply.
Leader-to-follower RPC that carries new entries plus the index and term of the entry before them (the consistency check); empty = heartbeat.
Vote only for a candidate whose log is at least as up-to-date as yours (later last term, or same last term and at least as long).

concepts: A majority elects and a majority commits; any two majorities overlap.
A log entry is identified by (index, term); matching (index, term) means matching prefixes.
Safety must not depend on timing; availability may.

codeWalkthrough.title: Randomized election timeout
codeWalkthrough.detail: `reset_timer()` draws 10-19 ticks from a per-node seeded RNG; a follower whose deadline passes becomes a candidate for `term + 1` and votes for itself. Randomness makes split votes (t=40) rare and short.

codeWalkthrough.title: Newer term wins
codeWalkthrough.detail: The first lines of `receive()`: any message with a higher term turns the receiver into a follower of that term and clears its vote. This is how a restarted old leader learns it is deposed.

codeWalkthrough.title: RequestVote
codeWalkthrough.detail: `granted = m['term'] == self.term and self.voted_for in (None, src)` — one vote per term. The lesson file stops here; the build task adds `(m['last_term'], m['last_index']) >= self.last()`.

codeWalkthrough.title: AppendEntries consistency check
codeWalkthrough.detail: A follower accepts only if it holds the entry at `prev_index` with `prev_term`; then it deletes any conflicting entry and everything after it and appends the rest. On refusal the leader decrements `next[p]` and retries.

codeWalkthrough.title: Commit rule
codeWalkthrough.detail: The leader scans from its last index down: the first N stored on a majority (`1 + sum(match >= N)`) whose entry has the leader's current term becomes the commit index (paper 5.4.2). Followers copy `min(leader commit, last new index)`.

codeWalkthrough.title: Persistent vs volatile state
codeWalkthrough.detail: `Cluster.restart()` keeps term, vote and log (as if on disk) but resets role and commit index; the node relearns the commit index from the leader.

codeWalkthrough.title: Safety checker
codeWalkthrough.detail: `helpers.SafetyChecker` remembers the first committed entry per index and reports any node that later has something else there — the State Machine Safety property as a test oracle.

title: Network partitions and fault injection: proxy toxics, split brain, fencing and linearizability checking
description: A Toxiproxy-style proxy cuts one node off the lease store; two nodes believe they lead and both write; a Jepsen-style history check proves clients saw something impossible until storage checks fencing tokens.
outcome: You can inject partitions, delays and drops between components, record a client history as JSON lines, check it for linearizability, and close the split-brain write path with fencing tokens.
environment: Python 3.12 (validated on 3.12.15, Linux), stdlib only, no installs beyond lesson 1; macOS (Apple silicon) and Windows 11: same commands (env-var syntax differs, see steps). Optional: Toxiproxy 2.13.0 and Maelstrom 0.2.4 (manual); agent assist uses the vendored fake model server (or Ollama).
overview: A partition turns 'the leader' into two leaders for a while; only a check at the shared resource (fencing) or a history checker that looks at what clients saw will tell you.

glossary.meaning: Toxiproxy's word for a fault applied to one direction of a proxied link: latency, timeout, reset_peer, packet loss...; 'down' = proxy disabled.
Two nodes act as leader at the same time because they cannot see each other or the arbiter.
The list of client operations with invoke and completion times and results (Jepsen style).
Every operation appears to take effect at one instant between its start and end, as if on a single copy.

concepts: To the caller, 'down' and 'slow' look the same: a timeout.
Check the client history, not just the final state.
Fencing makes stale writes fail; it does not make stale reads correct.

codeWalkthrough.title: Leader-local reads
codeWalkthrough.detail: `handle()` answers reads from `self.cache` — fast, and correct only while the node really leads. That is why n2's read returns 2 after n1 wrote 3.

codeWalkthrough.title: Write path

title: Sagas with compensation: orchestration vs choreography, idempotent steps, saga log
description: An order saga across orders, payments and shipping: when shipping fails (seeded) the lesson orchestrator keeps the customer's money; you add reverse-order, idempotent compensation and crash recovery from the saga log.
outcome: You can design a saga with compensating actions, keep every step and compensation idempotent, recover a crashed orchestrator from its log, and compare orchestration with choreography.
environment: Python 3.12 (validated on 3.12.15, Linux), stdlib only, no installs beyond lesson 1; macOS (Apple silicon) and Windows 11: same commands (env-var syntax differs, see steps).
overview: Without a distributed transaction, a failed late step must be undone by compensating actions, newest first — and recovery after a crash will run some of them twice, so they must be idempotent.

glossary.meaning: A sequence of local transactions T1..Tn; if one fails, compensations Cj..C1 undo the completed ones (Garcia-Molina & Salem, 1987).
A semantic undo (refund, cancel) recorded as a new change, not a rollback.
One coordinator calls each step / each service reacts to events and publishes the next.
Durable record of every step's status; the source of truth for recovery.

concepts: Undo completed steps in reverse order.
Every step and every compensation is idempotent and keyed by the saga id.
A step whose outcome is unknown after a crash is 'in doubt': compensate it (safe because idempotent).

title: Distributed tracing with W3C traceparent: propagation, spans as JSON lines, critical path
description: Three stdlib HTTP services propagate W3C traceparent and record spans as JSON lines; an analyzer rebuilds the trace and its critical path — until one hop drops the header and the trace breaks in two.
outcome: You can propagate trace context across HTTP hops, validate traceparent per the W3C spec, rebuild a trace from spans, find the critical path, and fix propagation once in middleware.
environment: Python 3.12 (validated on 3.12.15, Linux), stdlib only, no installs beyond lesson 1; macOS (Apple silicon) and Windows 11: same commands (env-var syntax differs, see steps). Optional (pending-ci): opentelemetry-api / -sdk / -exporter-otlp-proto-http 1.45.1 for otel_equivalent.py; Jaeger 2.22.0 (manual).
overview: A trace is only as good as its weakest hop: every service must continue the incoming trace id and pass its own span id on, ideally in middleware so no call site can forget.

glossary.meaning: One unit of work (here: one request handled by one service) with start, end, its own id and its parent's id.
W3C header `version-traceid-parentid-flags`, e.g. 00-4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-00f067aa0ba902b7-01.
The chain of spans that decides when the request finishes; shortening anything else does not help.
A span's duration minus the time covered by its children on the critical path.

concepts: Continue the incoming trace id; send your own span id as the next parent id.
Invalid or missing header -> start a new trace (and count how often).
Propagate in middleware, not at each call site.

code:
"""L300 lesson 15 (python tracing.py): W3C Trace Context across three stdlib HTTP services on 127.0.0.1.
gateway /checkout -> orders /create -> payments /authorize, then gateway -> payments /receipt. Every service
records a span (JSON lines); analyze.py groups them into traces and finds the critical path.
Happy path: one trace, four spans. Fault: one hop forgets the traceparent header -> the trace breaks in two."""
import json, random, re, threading, time

from analyze import critical_path, problems, traces
from helpers import QuietHandler, call, serve

TRACEPARENT = re.compile(r"^([0-9a-f]{2})-([0-9a-f]{32})-([0-9a-f]{16})-([0-9a-f]{2})(-.*)?$")  # version-trace-parent-flags
WORK = {"/checkout": 0.005, "/create": 0.02, "/authorize": 0.06, "/receipt": 0.01}  # seconds of fake work
URL, SPANS, LOCK, CURRENT = {}, [], threading.Lock(), threading.local()
RNG = random.Random(15)  # seeded ids so runs are comparable; production ids come from a CSPRNG


def new_id(bits):
    with LOCK:
        return f"{RNG.getrandbits(bits):0{bits // 4}x}"


def parse_traceparent(value):
    """'00-<32 hex trace-id>-<16 hex parent-id>-<2 hex flags>' -> (trace_id, parent_id, flags), else None.
    All-zero ids, version ff and extra fields on version 00 are invalid; a higher version keeps its first four
    fields (W3C 3.2.4). An invalid or missing header means: start a NEW trace (W3C section 4)."""
    m = TRACEPARENT.match((value or "").strip())
    if not m or m[1] == "ff" or (m[1] == "00" and m[5]) or m[2] == "0" * 32 or m[3] == "0" * 16:
        return None
    return m[2], m[3], m[4]


def traced_call(url):
    """Client side of propagation: send MY span id as the callee's parent-id, same trace-id and flags
    (the caller's sampled flag passes on unchanged: this service never makes its own sampling decision)."""
    ctx = getattr(CURRENT, "span", None)
    headers = {"traceparent": f"00-{ctx['trace_id']}-{ctx['span_id']}-{CURRENT.flags}"} if ctx else {}
    return call(url, headers=headers)


class Service(QuietHandler):
    name, routes = "service", {}

    def do_GET(self):
        incoming = parse_traceparent(self.headers.get("traceparent"))  # header names are case-insensitive
        trace_id, parent_id, flags = incoming or (new_id(128), None, "01")  # new trace: sampled
        span = {"trace_id": trace_id, "span_id": new_id(64), "parent_id": parent_id, "service": self.name,
                "name": f"GET {self.path}", "start": time.perf_counter()}
        CURRENT.span, CURRENT.flags = span, flags  # server middleware: this request is the current context
        try:
            status, body = self.routes[self.path](self)
        finally:
            span["end"], CURRENT.span = time.perf_counter(), None
            with LOCK:
                SPANS.append(span)
        self.reply(status, body)


class Gateway(Service):
    name = "gateway"
    routes = {"/checkout": lambda h: (time.sleep(WORK["/checkout"]), traced_call(URL["orders"] + "/create"),
                                      traced_call(URL["payments"] + "/receipt"), (200, {"ok": True}))[-1]}


class Orders(Service):
    name = "orders"
    # BUG on purpose: a raw call() - written before tracing existed - so this hop sends no traceparent
    routes = {"/create": lambda h: (time.sleep(WORK["/create"]), call(URL["payments"] + "/authorize"), (200, {}))[-1]}


class Payments(Service):
    name = "payments"
    routes = {"/authorize": lambda h: (time.sleep(WORK["/authorize"]), (200, {}))[-1],
              "/receipt": lambda h: (time.sleep(WORK["/receipt"]), (200, {}))[-1]}


def run_checkout(services=(Gateway, Orders, Payments), headers=None):
    """Start the three services, send one checkout, stop them. Returns the spans as dicts (times in ms)."""
    SPANS.clear()
    servers = {cls.name: serve(cls) for cls in services}
    URL.update({name: f"http://127.0.0.1:{srv.server_port}" for name, srv in servers.items()})
    call(URL["gateway"] + "/checkout", headers=headers)
    for srv in servers.values():
        srv.shutdown()
        srv.server_close()
    t0 = min(s["start"] for s in SPANS)
    return [{**s, "start": round((s["start"] - t0) * 1000, 1), "end": round((s["end"] - t0) * 1000, 1)} for s in SPANS]


if __name__ == "__main__":
    spans = run_checkout()
    print("spans (JSON lines, one per request):", *(json.dumps(s) for s in sorted(spans, key=lambda s: s["start"])), sep="\n  ")
    for trace_id, members in traces(spans).items():
        print(f"trace {trace_id[:8]}..: {len(members)} span(s):", ", ".join(f"{s['service']} {s['name']}" for s in members))
    root = min((s for s in spans if s["parent_id"] is None), key=lambda s: s["start"])
    print("critical path:", " | ".join(f"{s['service']} {s['name']} self {ms:.0f} ms" for s, ms in critical_path(spans, root)))
    print("trace problems:", *(problems(spans) or ["none"]), sep="\n  ")

codeWalkthrough.title: Strict parsing
codeWalkthrough.detail: `TRACEPARENT` + `parse_traceparent` accept lowercase hex only; all-zero trace or parent ids, version `ff` and extra fields on version 00 are rejected, while a higher version keeps its first four fields (W3C 3.2.4). Invalid -> `None` -> new trace, as the W3C processing model says.

codeWalkthrough.title: Server middleware
codeWalkthrough.detail: `Service.do_GET` parses the header, starts a span (new span id, parent = incoming parent-id), stores it and the incoming trace-flags in the thread-local `CURRENT` (a new trace gets `01`, sampled), runs the route and records the span — every service gets this without writing tracing code.

codeWalkthrough.title: Client propagation
codeWalkthrough.detail: `traced_call` sends `00-<same trace id>-<my span id>-<incoming flags>`, so the callee's span becomes my child and the caller's sampling decision (`01` sampled, `00` not) travels on unchanged.

codeWalkthrough.title: The broken hop
codeWalkthrough.detail: `Orders.routes` uses the raw `call()` — no header — so payments starts a new trace with `parent_id: null`.

codeWalkthrough.title: Spans as JSON lines
codeWalkthrough.detail: Each span is one dict (trace_id, span_id, parent_id, service, name, start, end); the demo prints them as JSON lines, the format a collector would ingest.

codeWalkthrough.title: Analysis
codeWalkthrough.detail: `analyze.traces` groups by trace id; `critical_path` walks back from the root's end through the last-finishing children; `problems` flags extra roots and orphan parents.

title: Backpressure and load shedding: bounded queues, 503 + Retry-After, AIMD concurrency limits
description: A 4-worker server under open-model load: queueing delay vs throughput measured, then a 150% burst makes an unbounded queue's p99 explode; a bounded queue that sheds with 503 + Retry-After keeps p99 near 160 ms.
outcome: You can measure queueing delay against throughput, explain why unbounded queues turn bursts into long outages, add admission control with 503 + Retry-After, and use an AIMD concurrency limit on the caller.
environment: Python 3.12 (validated on 3.12.15, Linux), stdlib only, no installs beyond lesson 1; macOS (Apple silicon) and Windows 11: same commands (env-var syntax differs, see steps). Optional: Grafana k6 v2.3.0 against serve_realtime.py (manual).
overview: Throughput stops at capacity but waiting does not: bound the queue to bound latency, and answer the excess quickly with 503 + Retry-After.

glossary.meaning: Requests arrive at a rate independent of how fast the server answers (real users, k6 arrival-rate executors).
Answers that arrive while the client is still waiting (here: within 1 s).
Refusing work early (503) so the work you accept finishes in time.
Additive increase, multiplicative decrease: grow a limit slowly on success, cut it fast on overload (TCP congestion control).

concepts: Little's law: requests in system = arrival rate x time in system.
Near capacity, waiting grows much faster than load.
Bound every queue by a latency budget, not by memory.

code:
"""L300 lesson 16 (python backpressure.py): a server with 4 workers (10 ms per request on average, so capacity
is 400 requests/s) and a queue in front of them. Open-model load (Poisson, seeded): clients keep sending no
matter how slow the server gets. Part 1 measures queueing delay vs throughput as load approaches capacity.
Part 2 is the fault: a 10 s burst at 150% of capacity, with per-second metrics as JSON lines.
The lesson server's queue is unbounded - watch p99 and how long the server stays slow after the burst."""
import json
from collections import deque

from helpers import simulate

WORKERS, SERVICE_MS = 4, 10.0
CAPACITY = WORKERS * 1000 / SERVICE_MS  # 400 requests/s
TIMEOUT_MS = 1000  # clients give up after 1 s: work finished later is wasted


class Server:
    def __init__(self, workers=WORKERS):
        self.workers, self.queue = workers, deque()

    def admit(self, now):
        """Admission control: return None to queue the request, or Retry-After seconds to shed it with a 503."""
        return None  # unbounded queue: everything waits, however long the line already is


def pct(values, p):
    values = sorted(values)
    return values[min(len(values) - 1, int(p / 100 * len(values)))] if values else 0.0


def summary(records):
    ok = [r for r in records if r["status"] == 200]
    lat = [r["end"] - r["arrive"] for r in ok]
    secs = (max(r["end"] for r in records) - min(r["arrive"] for r in records)) / 1000
    return {"offered": len(records), "ok": len(ok), "shed": sum(r["status"] == 503 for r in records),
            "throughput_per_s": round(len(ok) / secs), "mean_wait_ms": round(sum(r["start"] - r["arrive"] for r in ok) / max(1, len(ok)), 1),
            "p50_ms": round(pct(lat, 50), 1), "p99_ms": round(pct(lat, 99), 1),
            "goodput": sum(l <= TIMEOUT_MS for l in lat)}  # answered before the client gave up


def per_second(records):
    """Metrics a dashboard would scrape: one JSON line per second of arrival time."""
    lines = []
    for sec in range(int(max(r["arrive"] for r in records) // 1000) + 1):
        rs = [r for r in records if sec * 1000 <= r["arrive"] < (sec + 1) * 1000]
        lat = [r["end"] - r["arrive"] for r in rs if r["status"] == 200]
        lines.append(json.dumps({"t": sec, "offered": len(rs), "ok": len(lat), "shed": sum(r["status"] == 503 for r in rs),
                                 "p99_ms": round(pct(lat, 99))}))
    return lines


BURST = [(5, 0.6 * CAPACITY), (10, 1.5 * CAPACITY), (15, 0.6 * CAPACITY)]

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(f"capacity {CAPACITY:.0f} requests/s ({WORKERS} workers x {SERVICE_MS:.0f} ms)")
    print("1) load sweep, 20 s each:  load  throughput/s  mean wait  p99")
    for load in (0.5, 0.8, 0.9, 0.95):
        s = summary(simulate(Server(), [(20, load * CAPACITY)], SERVICE_MS))
        print(f"{load:>28.0%} {s['throughput_per_s']:>10} {s['mean_wait_ms']:>9} ms {s['p99_ms']:>6} ms")
    records = simulate(Server(), BURST, SERVICE_MS)
    print("2) burst: 5 s at 60%, 10 s at 150%, 15 s at 60% - per-second metrics (JSON lines):")
    print(*per_second(records)[3:30:3], sep="\n")
    print("summary:", json.dumps(summary(records)))

codeWalkthrough.title: Capacity
codeWalkthrough.detail: `CAPACITY = WORKERS * 1000 / SERVICE_MS` = 400 requests/s; every number in the lab is read against it.

codeWalkthrough.title: Admission control hook
codeWalkthrough.detail: `Server.admit(now)` returns None (queue it) or a Retry-After in seconds (shed with 503). The lesson version always returns None: an unbounded queue.

codeWalkthrough.title: Open-model engine
codeWalkthrough.detail: `helpers.simulate` pre-generates Poisson arrivals per load segment and exponential service times from one seeded RNG; free workers take the oldest queued request.

codeWalkthrough.title: p99 and goodput
codeWalkthrough.detail: `summary()` reports p50/p99 of successful requests and goodput (answered within TIMEOUT_MS = 1 s). An unbounded queue has 0 errors and terrible goodput.

codeWalkthrough.title: Metrics as JSON lines
codeWalkthrough.detail: `per_second()` buckets requests by arrival second: offered, ok, shed, p99 — what you would scrape into a dashboard.

codeWalkthrough.title: The burst profile
codeWalkthrough.detail: `BURST` = 5 s at 60%, 10 s at 150%, 15 s at 60%: the backlog grows by ~200 requests/s and drains at only 160/s afterwards.
